chapter.title: When your legs shake

cards.body: You're at the start of the walk, and your legs are shaking. Your body has got the wrong idea: it thinks you're about to run from something, not stroll with friends. **Nerves are your body getting ready to run.** Fast breath, dry mouth, a heart you can hear. None of it means you're unready. It means your body turned up early, dressed for the wrong kind of walk.
cards.simpler: You are about to start the walk, and your legs are shaking. Your body has got the wrong idea. It thinks you are about to run from something, not take a stroll with friends. **Nerves are your body getting ready to run.** Your breath goes fast. Your mouth goes dry. You can hear your own heart. None of this means you are not ready. It means your body showed up early, dressed for the wrong kind of walk.

cards.prompt: Priya is about to give a 3-minute talk about her sourdough starter to 6 colleagues. Her mouth is dry, her breath is quick, and the words in her head are speeding up. What is her body doing?

options.text: Telling her she hasn't prepared enough.
Getting ready to run, as if there were danger.
Running out of energy before she starts.

whyNot.a: That's the story the mind adds, not what the body is doing: a dry mouth shows up in people who have rehearsed 10 times too.
whyNot.c: That's the opposite: nerves give you too much energy, not too little, which is why everything speeds up.

cards.reteach: Nerves are not a verdict on your talk. They are your body flipping into run-from-danger mode: breath fast, mouth dry, speech quick. It got ready for the wrong kind of walk, that's all.

cards.title: What nerves actually do
cards.body:
Your body cannot tell a room of 6 colleagues from a dog chasing you. In both cases it flips the same switch, *run-from-danger mode*, and does 3 things. It breathes faster, to get oxygen for running. It stops making spit, because digesting is not urgent right now. It speeds everything up, including your mouth.

So what you feel is not random. **Fast breath, dry mouth and racing speech are one event**, not three problems. They come from the same switch.

That is good news. One switch means one lever. You don't have to talk yourself calm. You can reach the switch through the body.
cards.simpler: Your body cannot tell a room of 6 colleagues from a dog chasing you. Both flip the same switch, run-from-danger mode, and it does 3 things. You breathe faster, to get air for running. You stop making spit, because digesting can wait. Everything speeds up, including your talking. **Fast breath, dry mouth and racing speech are one event**, not three problems. One switch means one lever. You don't need to talk yourself calm. Reach the switch through the body.

cards.title: The out-breath and the champagne
cards.body: Picture Tom, a nurse who hands over to 8 colleagues at 7am without a flicker, shaking so hard at his sister's wedding toast that the champagne makes a small wave. Same man, same mouth, different switch. So 2 minutes before, he stands by the kitchen door and breathes in for a count of 4 and out for a count of 6, 8 times. **The out-breath being longer than the in-breath is the part that matters**: it is the body's own signal that the danger has passed. The toast is fine, and the champagne stays in the glass.
cards.simpler: Tom is a nurse. He hands over to 8 colleagues at 7am without a flicker. At his sister's wedding toast, he shakes so hard the champagne makes a small wave. Two minutes before, he stands by the kitchen door and breathes in for 4, out for 6, 8 times. **The out-breath being longer than the in-breath is the part that matters.** It tells the body the danger has passed. The toast is fine. The champagne stays in the glass.

cards.prompt: It's 2 minutes before Dev's talk at the book club. His heart is loud. Which move actually reaches the switch?

options.text: Read his notes again, fast, to be sure he knows them.
Tell himself firmly that there's nothing to be scared of.
Breathe in for 4, out for 6, about 8 times, with both feet flat on the floor.

whyNot.a: That's prep, not calming: reading fast at this point only feeds the speed.
whyNot.b: That's arguing with the mind, not the body: the switch doesn't understand words, it understands breath.

cards.reteach: The switch that makes your heart loud was flipped by the body, so it answers to the body. A slow out-breath, longer than the in-breath, is the clearest 'safe now' signal you can send. Words don't reach it.

cards.title: The 2-minute routine
cards.body:
Here are the 3 physical things, in order, for the 2 minutes before you stand up.

First, breathe. In through the nose for 4, out through the mouth for 6. Do it 8 to 10 times. **The long out-breath is the whole trick.** If 6 feels long, 5 is fine. Longer out than in is the rule.

Second, plant. Both feet flat, about shoulder-width apart, and press them into the floor for 5 seconds. Shaking legs calm down when they have a job.

Third, wet your mouth. One small sip of water, and keep the glass where you can reach it. Dry mouth is the symptom people hear most, and the easiest to fix.
cards.simpler: Three things for the 2 minutes before you stand up. First, breathe. In through the nose for 4, out through the mouth for 6, 8 to 10 times. **The long out-breath is the whole trick.** Second, plant. Both feet flat, shoulder-width apart, pressed into the floor for 5 seconds. Shaking legs settle when they have a job. Third, sip some water and keep the glass close. Dry mouth is what people hear most, and the easiest to fix.

cards.body: Maya felt her heart racing 10 minutes before her talk and decided the fix was to get it over with. She asked to go first, walked up fast, and started speaking at the pace of her heartbeat. The room heard a sprint. **Nerves make you want to hurry, and hurrying feeds the nerves.** You spot it when you notice you skipped the pause before your first sentence. That missing pause is the tell.
cards.simpler: Maya felt her heart racing 10 minutes before her talk. She decided the fix was to get it over with. She asked to go first, walked up fast, and started speaking at the pace of her heartbeat. The room heard a sprint. **Nerves make you want to hurry, and hurrying feeds the nerves.** How do you spot it? You notice you skipped the pause before your first sentence. That missing pause is the giveaway.

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'I get a dry mouth before I speak, so I must just be a bad speaker.' What's the sharpest reply from this chapter?

options.text: Dry mouth is your body stopping spit to get ready to run. It says nothing about your talk, and a sip of water fixes it.
Dry mouth means you've been talking too much already. Rest your voice.
Dry mouth comes from staring at your notes too long. Put the notes away.

whyNot.b: That's a tired voice, not nerves: this dry mouth arrives before you've said a word.
whyNot.c: That's a guess at the cause, not the cause: notes don't dry your mouth, the run-from-danger switch does.

cards.reteach: Every nerve symptom, including dry mouth, comes from one switch: the body preparing to run. That switch is not a judge of your talk. You turn it down with a long out-breath, planted feet and a sip of water.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Nerves are your body getting ready to run, which is why your breath, mouth and speech all speed up at once. **In the 2 minutes before, breathe out longer than you breathe in**, plant your feet, sip water, and your body gets the message before your mind does.
cards.simpler: Nerves are your body getting ready to run. That is why your breath, your mouth and your speech all speed up at the same time. **In the 2 minutes before, breathe out longer than you breathe in.** Then plant your feet and sip some water. Your body gets the message before your mind does.

cards.body: Tonight, before a phone call you'd rather not make, breathe in for 4 and out for 6, 8 times. Notice whether your first sentence comes out slower than usual.
cards.simpler: Try this tonight. Pick a phone call you would rather not make. Before you dial, breathe in for a count of 4 and out for a count of 6. Do that 8 times. Then make the call. **Notice whether your first sentence comes out slower than usual.** That is the whole test.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now name what nerves do to your body and slow your heart with a 4-in, 6-out breath in the 2 minutes before you stand up.
